The monsoon had flooded half the roads in Chandigarh, and Jasleen's friend Simar was still having her birthday party, till eleven, at a farmhouse outside the city.

"No," said her father, Madhav, before she'd finished asking.

"Papa, everyone's going. Simar's mum will be there."

"The roads are underwater. It's far. It's late. No."

Jasleen stood in the doorway, feeling like a small child. She was fifteen. She'd been getting herself to school for years, gone alone to the tuition office, looked after her little brother. Didn't any of that count?

Madhav turned back to the news, jaw tight. He didn't say what he was picturing: the car in a flooded underpass, his phone ringing at midnight. He only said, "Maybe next time."

She went to her room. He turned up the volume, and didn't hear a word of the news.

qa.a: At a farmhouse outside the city.

qa.q: How does Jasleen feel standing in the doorway?
qa.a: She feels small and unseen, treated like a child even though she handles many things on her own.

qa.q: What could Madhav try, instead of just "No"?
qa.a: He could say what actually frightens him, the flooded roads and a late call, and discuss options, like an earlier pickup.

qa.q: What is Madhav feeling as he turns up the volume?
qa.a: He is anxious and fearful, picturing the flooded underpass, but he can't quite put that fear into words.

grounding: Jasleen wants to go to a late party and her father says no; she feels her growing independence unseen while he holds a fear he cannot voice.

Aparna came in at 9:40, forty minutes past curfew, and her father, Nitin, was waiting in the hall of their Indore flat.

"Where were you?"

"At Riddhi's. I told you. We were finishing the project."

"You were supposed to be home by nine. From now on, straight home after school. That's final."

"Because I said so."

"You never trust me! It was forty minutes!"

"Don't raise your voice at me."

"You raised yours first!"

Aparna slammed her bag down. Nitin felt his chest tighten: for forty minutes he had been calling her phone and imagining things he didn't want to imagine. But all he could say was, "Go to your room."

Aparna went, thinking: he doesn't care what I did, only that I obeyed. Neither of them said the thing that was true.

It started with Gopika asking to go to the mall on Sunday. It ended somewhere else entirely.

"The mall?" said her father, Nilesh, putting down the newspaper in their Vadodara flat. "With your marks? You got fifty-two in maths."

"That was one test, Papa."

"And last month you told us you were at the library when you were at Rinki's. Remember that lie?"

"Oh, here we go. Bring up everything I've ever done."

"Don't be sarcastic with me."

"Sure. Sorry, sir. Anything else from Class 6 you'd like to discuss?"

Nilesh's voice went up. He talked about sacrifices, tuition fees, the neighbours' daughter who topped the district. Gopika rolled her eyes so hard it hurt.

Twenty minutes later, nobody remembered the mall. Nilesh was hoarse. Gopika was in tears of fury. And neither of them had said a single true thing about how they felt.

qa.a: Fifty-two.

qa.a: Old failures were dragged in and the mall question was lost; sticking to Sunday's plan and naming the real worry would have helped.

The fight was supposed to be about my phone bill. By the end, it was about everything.

Mumma saw the data charges and said, "Pallavi, this is too much." Fair. But then she said, "And your marks were terrible, and you lied about the sleepover last month, and your friend Shreya is a bad influence."

Tanuja, you asked why I'm always so quick to make up after a fight with your mother. Let me, your Nazia nani, tell you a story.

When I was fifteen, I had a terrible fight with my own Ammi over a school trip. I slammed my door. She went silent. For three days, we didn't speak.

I stayed in my room. She cooked and cleaned and didn't knock. We both felt misunderstood. And, if I'm honest, a little ashamed of what we'd said.

The worst part was my little brother Kamran. He ate his meals quietly, looking from one of us to the other. He stopped laughing. He even stopped playing his cricket in the courtyard.

Each of us waited for the other to give in first.

It was only when Kamran cried at dinner that Ammi and I looked at each other properly. That was the turning point.

The power had been out since the afternoon, and in the two-room flat in Patna there was nowhere to hide from a fight.

Charu sat on her bed with a torch, pretending to read. Her mother sat in the kitchen with a candle, not cooking. Neither had said a word since Charu shouted, "You never let me do anything!" and her mother replied, "Then do whatever you want," and walked away.

In the middle, on the floor, her little brother Jatin was trying to do his homework by phone light. He kept looking from one room to the other.

"Didi, are you and Mummy fighting?"

"No."

"Then why is nobody talking?"

Charu didn't answer. She felt misunderstood, and underneath that, a small shame about how loud she'd been.

In the kitchen her mother felt the same. Each waited for the other to speak first. Jatin gave up on his homework and lay down between them, very quiet.

They'd fought about Darshan wanting to drop science for arts. Jagdish had said, "Out of the question. I won't discuss it." Darshan had said, "You never listen," and cut the call.

Jagdish took a breath. "Beta, I was scared on the phone, and I said it badly. I'm sorry. I'd like to hear what you want. And then I'll tell you what worries me. Can we do that?"

I'm sliding this under your door because I'm not sure you'll open it if I knock, and that's fair.

Last night I said you couldn't go on the cycling trip to Lonavala, and when you argued, I said, "This discussion is over." Then I said something about your marks that had nothing to do with the trip. I'm sorry.

I'd like to try again. Can we sit down tomorrow after dinner? You tell me what you want and why it matters to you, and I'll listen properly, all the way through. Then I'll tell you what worries me, and we'll see if there's a way.

You want to know what changed things with my son? I'm Madhav, Vikas's father, and I'll tell you straight: I knocked first.

Vikas wanted to go to a concert in Mumbai with friends. Overnight. I said no, loudly, and added a few things about his attitude. He said I treated him like a baby. Doors slammed. Two days of silence.

On the third night, I stood outside his room for about five minutes before I knocked. Then I said, "Vikas, I was scared and I said it badly. Can we talk about what you want, and what worries me?"

He opened the door, looking suspicious. I sat on his bed and let him talk. He told me about the band, the friends, the plan for where they'd stay. I didn't interrupt.

Then I told him my fear: the crowds, the late train. He actually listened. My son, who'd been rolling his eyes for months.

People ask how we stopped fighting about curfew in our house. I'm Ramesh, Zainab's father, and honestly, we made a deal.

Zainab wanted to stay out till ten on weekends with her friends from the theatre group. I wanted her home by eight. We'd fought about it for months.

So one Sunday we sat at the dining table with paper. We agreed: nine thirty on Saturdays. She'd text me when she reached the venue and when she left. If plans changed, she'd call, not text. And we'd review it after four weeks.

The first two weeks, she was back at nine twenty-five, every time. Third week, she called: "The rehearsal's running late, can I come at nine forty-five?" I said yes. That call mattered more than the time.

At the review, we moved it to ten. She earned it. And I learned to let her practise, even when my stomach was in knots.

qa.q: What time did they agree on for Saturdays at first?
qa.a: Nine thirty.

qa.q: How did Ramesh feel letting Zainab practise the new freedom?
qa.a: He felt anxious, his stomach in knots, but proud when she proved reliable.

qa.q: Why did the review after four weeks work well?
qa.a: It let Zainab show reliability and earn more freedom, while Ramesh kept a boundary and still let her practise.

qa.q: What did the phone call in the third week show about Zainab?
qa.a: It showed she was taking the agreement seriously, being honest when plans changed rather than just coming home late.

grounding: Ramesh and his daughter Zainab agree on a curfew, a contact plan and a review; her reliability earns more freedom and he learns to hold a boundary while letting her practise.

For weeks it was shouting. Hrithik wanted to go to his friends' gaming nights until eleven. Papa said nine, or nothing.

Then one Sunday, they sat on the balcony with a notebook. I pretended to do homework nearby. They wrote down: ten o'clock on Fridays. Hrithik would send a message when he reached and when he left. Papa would not call him every half hour. And they'd check again in a month.

For the first few Fridays, Hrithik was home at 9:55. Once he was late by fifteen minutes, but he'd called at 9:45 to say the auto was delayed. Papa didn't shout.

At the one-month check, Papa said, "You've been reliable. Let's make it ten thirty." Hrithik looked surprised, and then very pleased.

June. After another fight about Yogesh coming home late from football, his mother, Indu, sat him down at the kitchen table in their Jaipur flat. They wrote down a deal: home by seven thirty on weekdays; message when leaving the ground; if he'd be late, call before seven. Review in three weeks.

July, the review. Indu said, "You've been reliable. Eight o'clock from now on." Yogesh grinned. "Really?"

"Really. But the call-before-seven rule stays."

I moved back home after my second year at college, and within a week, I was fifteen again.

"Charu, where are you going?" "Who is this Varun who keeps calling?" "Why are you back at ten?"

Varun is my lab partner. We're doing a project on water filters. I tried to explain that. Papa just looked at me over his glasses, like I'd said something suspicious.

At the hostel, I'd managed my own money, my own schedule, even a trip to Rishikesh with friends. At home, I had to report every movement like a prisoner on parole.

The worst part was that I could see Papa didn't mean it badly. One night he said, "For twenty years I knew where you were every minute. Now I don't. I don't know how to stop asking."

I didn't know what to say to that. It was the first honest thing either of us had said all summer.

qa.q: What project are Charu and Varun doing?
qa.a: A project on water filters.

qa.q: How did Charu feel being questioned at home?
qa.a: Charu felt frustrated and treated like a child, like a prisoner on parole, after managing independently at the hostel.

qa.q: What turning point does Papa's honest comment open up?
qa.a: It lets them talk openly about how both feel, so they can agree on how much Charu shares as an adult.

qa.q: What is it like for Papa to have Charu home as an adult?
qa.a: He feels unsure and anxious, used to knowing where Charu was every minute and not knowing how to let go.

grounding: Charu, home from college, is questioned about where she goes and whom she meets and feels treated as a child, while her father admits he doesn't know how to let go.

College counsellor's note, Tuesday

Gopika, a second-year student, came in today, tearful. She lives at home with her mother, Usha, and says she has to report every place she goes and every friend she meets. "She calls me four times if I'm late from the library. I'm twenty-one."

She said she loves her mother and feels guilty for being angry. She described her mother as a widow who has "been in charge of everything for twenty years."

We talked about how her mother's questions may come from fear and long habit rather than distrust, and about how Gopika could share some information willingly, which may reduce the questioning.

She agreed to try telling her mother her plans in the morning, before being asked, for two weeks, and to have one calm conversation about what feels respectful to both of them. We will meet again next Tuesday.

— Ms Fernandes, counsellor

qa.a: She feels angry and treated like a child, but also guilty because she loves her mother.

I told my parents about Zubin on a Sunday, after lunch, because I thought full stomachs might help. They didn't.

Mummy put her cup down. Papa looked at the wall. Then Mummy said, very quietly, "We sent you to that college. We took a loan. We turned down your chacha's help so no one could say anything. And now you want to marry a boy we've never met, from another community?"

I tried to explain: he's kind, he's studying law, his family is lovely. But I could see that every word sounded to them like I was rejecting everything they'd done for me.

Papa finally said, "We had a plan for you." That was the worst part. Not the anger. The plan. As if I were a project that had gone off course.

I wasn't rejecting them. I was choosing someone. I didn't know how to make them see the difference.

— Sarika

qa.a: Law.

qa.a: Sarika felt hurt most by Papa's words "We had a plan for you", feeling treated like a project that had gone off course.

Student counsellor's note, Friday

Pankaj, first-year engineering, came to see me today. He wants to switch to a design course next year. His father has said no.

Pankaj described the argument: his father reminded him that the family sold land to pay his coaching fees for two years, and that his grandfather had always wanted an engineer in the family. "If you leave engineering, you're telling us everything we did was for nothing."

Pankaj said he feels torn: grateful and guilty, but also sure he is unhappy. He cried when he said, "I'm not rejecting them. I just want to choose my own work."

We discussed how his father may be hearing the choice as a rejection of the family's sacrifice. I suggested Pankaj begin by thanking his father for what he gave up, before explaining his reasons. We will meet again next week.

— Saurabh Mehta, counsellor

Wednesday night

I got the job in Bengaluru. The one I've wanted since second year. I told Ammi and Abbu at dinner, and I was so happy I didn't see it coming.

Ammi put her spoon down. "Bengaluru? Alone? We thought you'd work here, near us. Near Sabina."

Sabina is my little sister. She's only twelve. Ammi's been saying for years that I'd help raise her.

Abbu said, "We didn't send you to college so you could leave." He didn't shout. He just looked tired.

And suddenly I felt like I'd done something terrible. Like choosing a job was the same as choosing to abandon them.

I'm not abandoning anyone. I'd come home every holiday. I'd call every day. But to them, Bengaluru sounds like goodbye.

I haven't accepted the offer yet. I have until Friday.

— Ayesha

Leela had been accepted into a master's programme in Hyderabad. She told her mother, Shalini, in the kitchen of their Coimbatore home, while Shalini was rolling chapatis.

Shalini didn't look up. "After all we have done for you. Your father's extra shifts. My gold. And now you'll leave us, just when your father's knees are bad?"

Leela's throat went tight. Guilt came first, fast and heavy: her father's knees, her mother's bare wrists where the bangles used to be. Then, right behind it, anger. She hadn't asked for any of it to be a debt.

"Amma, I love you both. I'm not leaving you. I'm going to study."

"It's the same thing."

"It's not." But her voice wobbled.

Shalini kept rolling. Leela stood there, loving her mother and wanting her own life, feeling that she was being asked to pick one. It didn't seem fair.

qa.q: Where was Leela accepted for her master's programme?
qa.a: In Hyderabad.

qa.q: What two feelings hit Leela when her mother spoke?
qa.a: First guilt, fast and heavy, about her parents' sacrifices, then anger that their help was being treated as a debt.

qa.q: What could Leela do to avoid being forced to choose?
qa.a: Acknowledge her parents' sacrifices, then explain calmly how she can study and still support them, perhaps with a plan for visits and help at home.

qa.q: What might Shalini be feeling as she keeps rolling chapatis?
qa.a: She may be afraid of losing Leela and worried about the family, so the fear comes out as guilt-laden words.

grounding: Leela hears "after all we have done for you" when she chooses to study away, feeling guilt and anger at being forced to choose between her parents and her own life.

The call from my mother came while Bhavna and I were eating momos outside the college gate in Shillong.

I'd told my parents the week before that I wanted to join an NGO in Guwahati after graduation instead of the government exam coaching they'd planned. Mom's voice on the phone was quiet. "After all we have done for you. Your father worked two jobs so you could study. And now you want to throw it away?"

I felt it in my stomach: guilt, heavy and old. Then anger, right behind it. I never asked them to make it a debt.

I said, "Mom, I love you. I'm not throwing anything away." She hung up.

Bhavna put her plate down. "You okay?"

"No. I feel like I'm being asked to choose between them and me. And I love them. That's what makes it so unfair."

She squeezed my hand. We didn't finish the momos.

— Lalremsiami

In the women's hostel of the university in Delhi, Sunday evening was call-home time. Nandini sat on her bed with her phone, and her roommate Mehak listened, pretending to read.

"Yes, Mummy, I'm eating. Classes are fine. No, nothing new."

There was plenty new. Nandini had joined the debate club, was thinking of switching to economics, and had been going out with a boy from her class. None of it made it into the call.

"Why do you never tell me anything anymore?" her mother asked.

"There's nothing to tell, Mummy."

After she hung up, Mehak said, "You didn't tell her about the debate."

"If I tell her one thing, she'll ask ten questions and then we'll fight. It's easier this way."

"Easier for you. But she doesn't even know who you are now."

Nandini didn't answer. She stared at the phone for a while.

qa.a: The debate club.

qa.a: She feels wary and tired of conflict, believing that sharing anything will lead to questions and a fight.

Dear Sabina,

You asked how things are with my parents. Honestly? Peaceful. Too peaceful.

Since the fight about my job last year, I've learned to share almost nothing. When Mummy asks about work, I say "fine". I didn't tell them I got promoted, because then they'd ask why I'm not moving back home. I didn't tell them about the pottery class, or the new flatmates, or that I've started running in the mornings.

No fights. It works.

But last Sunday on the phone Mummy said, "I feel like I'm talking to a stranger." And I realised she's right. She knows the girl who left home three years ago. She's never met the woman I am now.

I don't know how to let her in without letting the fights back in too. Maybe you have ideas. You're better at this than me.

Love,
Alka

You asked why I don't tell my parents much anymore. I'm Sudha, and I'll be honest with you.

After the huge fight over my course in first year, I made a rule for myself: keep it short. "College is fine." "Food is fine." "No, nothing new." And it worked. No more shouting on the phone.

My friend Jyoti was shocked when I told her. She tells her mother everything, even about crushes. I said, "That's your family. Mine turns everything into a fight."

But last month, my father called on my birthday and asked, "What do you like these days? I didn't know what to gift you." And I didn't know what to say. He didn't know I'd started painting. He didn't know my best friends' names.

Keeping the peace was easy. But I think it's made me a stranger in my own family.

qa.a: Painting.
